# Sidecar protocol schema

The protocol reference for client authors is [`../PROTOCOL.md`](../PROTOCOL.md): transport, negotiation, every command and event, error codes and compatibility rules. This page is about the schema file and how it is kept current.

`sidecar-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) of the Nexus sidecar protocol, version 1: the newline-delimited JSON a client exchanges with the Node sidecar. `$defs.SidecarEvent` is every message the sidecar sends, `$defs.SidecarCommand` every message a client sends. Each is a `oneOf` over the message variants, told apart by the constant `type`; every message also carries `v`, the protocol version.

The file is generated from the types in `cli/src/protocol.ts` by the TypeScript type checker. Do not edit it by hand: change the types, then regenerate.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_protocol_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/sidecar-v1.schema.json
node scripts/gen_protocol_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or the ledger is stale
```

`cli/test/protocol_schema.test.ts` runs the same comparison, so CI fails when a protocol type changes and the schema does not.

## Recording a version decision

`VERSIONS.json` is the version ledger: entries `{ "protocol", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last. The newest entry must carry the SHA-256 of the checked-in schema and the current `PROTOCOL_VERSION`. A type change therefore needs two things: a regenerated schema and a new ledger entry whose `note` states the decision, either the same version because the change is additive and compatible (a new optional field, a new message an older peer ignores), or a bumped `PROTOCOL_VERSION`. Append entries; leave earlier ones as they are.

## Extra properties are allowed

No object in the schema sets `additionalProperties: false`. A newer sidecar may add an optional field to an event, and an older client must ignore it, so a schema that forbade unknown fields would reject messages the protocol means to accept. Commands are open for the same reason in the other direction: `parseCommand` reads the fields it knows and drops the rest. The schema checks what is required and the type of every field it names. `additionalProperties` appears only where a type has an index signature, where it gives the type of every value.

A tuple (`ReceiptRow`) is the exception: its length is fixed, as in the type.

## What the generator does with each type

- An interface or type alias declared under `cli/src` is written once under `$defs` and referenced with `$ref`. An instantiated generic (`Pick<SlashSpec, ...>`) and an intersection that forms a message (`models.catalog`) are written out in place.
- A union of string literals is an `enum`; `T | null` is `anyOf` with `{"type": "null"}`; an optional property is left out of `required`.
- JSDoc comments on types and properties become `description`.
- Definitions, properties, `required` lists, enum values and variants are sorted, so the output is the same on every run.
- A type with no JSON form (a function, an enum, a tuple with optional elements) stops the generator with an error naming the property.

## Samples and recordings derived from the schema

- `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_schema_samples.jsonl` holds a minimal and a full sample of every message, generated from the schema by `node cli/scripts/gen_protocol_samples.mjs` (`--check` exits 1 when it is stale). The Rust client's tests parse the event samples, so regenerate it after regenerating the schema.
- `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_rust_commands.jsonl` holds the lines the Rust client serializes. A Rust test keeps it equal to the client's output (`NEXUS_UPDATE_PROTOCOL_FIXTURES=1 cargo test --bin nexus-tui rust_commands` rewrites it); `cli/test/protocol_parity.test.ts` validates it against the schema.
- `cli/test/fixtures/wire/*.json` are recorded sessions replayed against the real sidecar by `cli/test/protocol_wire.test.ts`. `NEXUS_WIRE_RECORD=1` on that test rewrites them from the sidecar's real output; `cli/test/helpers/wire_fixture.ts` documents the format.

## The `nexus run --json` document

`run-result-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of the one document `nexus run --json` prints (`RunJsonOutput` in `cli/src/run_contract.ts`: a result, or an error document without `turn`). It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder`, so everything above about open objects and type mapping applies to it.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_run_result_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/run-result-v1.schema.json
node scripts/gen_run_result_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `RUN_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule: the newest entry carries the SHA-256 of the checked-in schema and the current `RUN_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. An added optional member keeps the version; a removed or renamed member, or a changed type or meaning, bumps it. The schema covers every type the result reaches (`TurnResult`, `ValidationReceipt` and the rest), so a change to any of them needs a regenerated schema and an entry. `cli/test/run_json_contract.test.ts` runs the comparison. The manual (`docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, "`nexus run --json`") describes the document and the exit codes.

## The `nexus verify --json` document

`verify-result-v2.schema.json` is the current JSON Schema of the one document `nexus verify --json` prints and `--receipt <file>` writes (`VerifyJsonOutput` in `cli/src/verify_contract.ts`: a result with `verdict`, or an error document without one). It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder`; the two command-result generators share `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`. The v1 schema and its ledger entry remain as the prior contract.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_verify_result_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/verify-result-v<N>.schema.json
node scripts/gen_verify_result_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `VERIFY_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `VERIFY_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The schema reaches `VerificationEvidence` and `TypecheckEvidence` (`cli/src/core/turn.ts`) and the guard's classes and modes (`cli/src/security.ts`), so a change to any of them needs a regenerated schema and an entry here as well as for the run result. `cli/test/verify_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison, and every result document the `nexus verify` tests produce is validated against the schema. The manual (`docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, "`nexus verify`") describes the document and the exit codes.

## The audit bundle

`audit-bundle-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of the two documents an audit bundle carries (`AuditBundleDocument` in `cli/src/audit_contract.ts`): `manifest.json` (`AuditManifest`) and the detached signature envelope `manifest.sig.json` (`AuditSignatureEnvelope`). `audit-verify-result-v1.schema.json` is the schema of the one document a verification of a bundle prints (`AuditVerifyOutput`: a result with `result`, or an error document without one). Both are generated by the same `SchemaBuilder` through `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_audit_schema.mjs           # rewrite both schemas
node scripts/gen_audit_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when a schema or its ledger is stale
```

Their ledgers are `AUDIT_BUNDLE_VERSIONS.json` and `AUDIT_VERIFY_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `AUDIT_BUNDLE_SCHEMA_VERSION` and `AUDIT_VERIFY_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The bundle schema reaches `ChainLink` (`cli/src/core/hash_chain.ts`), so a change there needs a regenerated schema and an entry. `cli/test/audit_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison and pins the exit-code table (`AUDIT_EXIT_CODES`); every manifest written and every result produced in `cli/test/audit_bundle.test.ts` is validated against the schemas.

A schema describes a document's shape only. What makes a bundle verify is defined in `cli/src/core/audit_bundle.ts`: `manifest.json` is exactly the canonical JSON of the manifest (keys sorted at every depth, no whitespace) and one newline; a file's `sha256` is over its bytes; each entry of `files` is linked to the one before it with `linkRecord`; `root_sha256` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the manifest without that member. Optional `manifest.sig.json` signs the exact manifest bytes with an Ed25519 key and a domain separator. The public key is never embedded; verification is signed only when a caller supplies and matches its own trusted public key.

## The managed policy document

`policy-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of a managed policy document (`ManagedPolicyFile` in `cli/src/core/managed_policy.ts`, plan unit GV-1). A policy file is TOML (`policy.toml`); the schema describes the same data as a JSON document, with each table an object, for an operator's editor or linter. It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder` through `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_policy_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/policy-v1.schema.json
node scripts/gen_policy_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `POLICY_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The version rule is stricter than for the result documents: every added, removed or changed key bumps `POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSION`, because a reader refuses a policy whose version it does not support instead of ignoring what it does not know. `cli/test/managed_policy_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison, checks that the schema and the validator name the same tables and keys, and validates generated documents and every example of `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md` against both.

The schema describes shape only and is looser than the validator (`validatePolicyDocument`): like every schema here it never sets `additionalProperties: false`, so it does not reject an unknown table or key, which the validator does; it does not check the form of list items (a command prefix, a host name, an `mcp.allow` entry); and a whole number is `number`. A file that passes the schema may still be refused. `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md` describes the format, the tiers and the errors. In this change the policy is a library: `nexus` does not read a policy file yet.
[
  {
    "protocol": 1,
    "schemaSha256": "b2747ba8d5d56e8450df9c161b1c773b7beefd5c79ccd75fa07dfccda169b66a",
    "note": "First published schema of protocol v1, generated from cli/src/protocol.ts as it stood on release/v1.3.0. No wire change."
  },
  {
    "protocol": 1,
    "schemaSha256": "9cf30b58fb0f720ef8ecbf5f1a3d8ad5015ca0f842fee9131b9f7b4d017bb4bc",
    "note": "Add objective tool invocation budget exhaustion and accounting fields to turn results; additive protocol v1 change."
  },
  {
    "protocol": 1,
    "schemaSha256": "ec987e1083659ed595b68edea6f1707746fce82f6136ab7cc197d9dfa4d51037",
    "note": "Capability negotiation, additive, so the version stays 1. hello gains the optional fields protocol_min, protocol_max, capabilities and experimental; the new command initialize is answered by the new event initialized; error codes UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL and EXPERIMENTAL_DISABLED are added. An older client ignores the new hello fields and never sends initialize, so it sees what it saw before; a newer client that finds no range in hello falls back to the exact-version check, and one that sends initialize to an older sidecar gets BAD_REQUEST (unknown message type) and carries on without negotiation. No existing field or message changed meaning."
  }
]

- A type with no JSON form (a function, an enum, a tuple with optional elements) stops the generator with an error naming the property.

## Samples and recordings derived from the schema

- `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_schema_samples.jsonl` holds a minimal and a full sample of every message, generated from the schema by `node cli/scripts/gen_protocol_samples.mjs` (`--check` exits 1 when it is stale). The Rust client's tests parse the event samples, so regenerate it after regenerating the schema.
- `cli/test/fixtures/protocol_v1_rust_commands.jsonl` holds the lines the Rust client serializes. A Rust test keeps it equal to the client's output (`NEXUS_UPDATE_PROTOCOL_FIXTURES=1 cargo test --bin nexus-tui rust_commands` rewrites it); `cli/test/protocol_parity.test.ts` validates it against the schema.
- `cli/test/fixtures/wire/*.json` are recorded sessions replayed against the real sidecar by `cli/test/protocol_wire.test.ts`. `NEXUS_WIRE_RECORD=1` on that test rewrites them from the sidecar's real output; `cli/test/helpers/wire_fixture.ts` documents the format.

## The `nexus run --json` document

`run-result-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of the one document `nexus run --json` prints (`RunJsonOutput` in `cli/src/run_contract.ts`: a result, or an error document without `turn`). It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder`, so everything above about open objects and type mapping applies to it.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_run_result_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/run-result-v1.schema.json
node scripts/gen_run_result_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `RUN_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule: the newest entry carries the SHA-256 of the checked-in schema and the current `RUN_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. An added optional member keeps the version; a removed or renamed member, or a changed type or meaning, bumps it. The schema covers every type the result reaches (`TurnResult`, `ValidationReceipt` and the rest), so a change to any of them needs a regenerated schema and an entry. `cli/test/run_json_contract.test.ts` runs the comparison. The manual (`docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, "`nexus run --json`") describes the document and the exit codes.

## The `nexus verify --json` document

`verify-result-v2.schema.json` is the current JSON Schema of the one document `nexus verify --json` prints and `--receipt <file>` writes (`VerifyJsonOutput` in `cli/src/verify_contract.ts`: a result with `verdict`, or an error document without one). It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder`; the two command-result generators share `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`. The v1 schema and its ledger entry remain as the prior contract.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_verify_result_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/verify-result-v<N>.schema.json
node scripts/gen_verify_result_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `VERIFY_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `VERIFY_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The schema reaches `VerificationEvidence` and `TypecheckEvidence` (`cli/src/core/turn.ts`) and the guard's classes and modes (`cli/src/security.ts`), so a change to any of them needs a regenerated schema and an entry here as well as for the run result. `cli/test/verify_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison, and every result document the `nexus verify` tests produce is validated against the schema. The manual (`docs/USER_MANUAL.md`, "`nexus verify`") describes the document and the exit codes.

## The audit bundle

`audit-bundle-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of the two documents an audit bundle carries (`AuditBundleDocument` in `cli/src/audit_contract.ts`): `manifest.json` (`AuditManifest`) and the detached signature envelope `manifest.sig.json` (`AuditSignatureEnvelope`). `audit-verify-result-v1.schema.json` is the schema of the one document a verification of a bundle prints (`AuditVerifyOutput`: a result with `result`, or an error document without one). Both are generated by the same `SchemaBuilder` through `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_audit_schema.mjs           # rewrite both schemas
node scripts/gen_audit_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when a schema or its ledger is stale
```

Their ledgers are `AUDIT_BUNDLE_VERSIONS.json` and `AUDIT_VERIFY_RESULT_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `AUDIT_BUNDLE_SCHEMA_VERSION` and `AUDIT_VERIFY_RESULT_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The bundle schema reaches `ChainLink` (`cli/src/core/hash_chain.ts`), so a change there needs a regenerated schema and an entry. `cli/test/audit_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison and pins the exit-code table (`AUDIT_EXIT_CODES`); every manifest written and every result produced in `cli/test/audit_bundle.test.ts` is validated against the schemas.

A schema describes a document's shape only. What makes a bundle verify is defined in `cli/src/core/audit_bundle.ts`: `manifest.json` is exactly the canonical JSON of the manifest (keys sorted at every depth, no whitespace) and one newline; a file's `sha256` is over its bytes; each entry of `files` is linked to the one before it with `linkRecord`; `root_sha256` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the manifest without that member. Optional `manifest.sig.json` signs the exact manifest bytes with an Ed25519 key and a domain separator. The public key is never embedded; verification is signed only when a caller supplies and matches its own trusted public key.

## The managed policy document

`policy-v1.schema.json` is the JSON Schema of a managed policy document (`ManagedPolicyFile` in `cli/src/core/managed_policy.ts`, plan unit GV-1). A policy file is TOML (`policy.toml`); the schema describes the same data as a JSON document, with each table an object, for an operator's editor or linter. It is generated by the same `SchemaBuilder` through `cli/scripts/result_schema.mjs`.

```bash
cd cli
node scripts/gen_policy_schema.mjs           # rewrite docs/protocol/policy-v1.schema.json
node scripts/gen_policy_schema.mjs --check   # exit 1 when the schema or its ledger is stale
```

Its ledger is `POLICY_VERSIONS.json`, entries `{ "schema_version", "schemaSha256", "note" }`, newest last, under the same rule as the run-result ledger with `POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSION`. The version rule is stricter than for the result documents: every added, removed or changed key bumps `POLICY_SCHEMA_VERSION`, because a reader refuses a policy whose version it does not support instead of ignoring what it does not know. `cli/test/managed_policy_schema.test.ts` runs the comparison, checks that the schema and the validator name the same tables and keys, and validates generated documents and every example of `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md` against both.

The schema describes shape only and is looser than the validator (`validatePolicyDocument`): like every schema here it never sets `additionalProperties: false`, so it does not reject an unknown table or key, which the validator does; it does not check the form of list items (a command prefix, a host name, an `mcp.allow` entry); and a whole number is `number`. A file that passes the schema may still be refused. `docs/MANAGED_POLICY.md` describes the format, the tiers and the errors. In this change the policy is a library: `nexus` does not read a policy file yet.

       xerj corpus own <name> [--off]
       xerj corpus build <name> [--recipe <path>] [--fresh]
       xerj corpus sign <pack-dir> --key <seed-file>
       xerj corpus keygen --out <prefix>
       xerj corpus index <name> [--fresh] [--url URL] [--include-data]
         (can outlive an agent tool timeout; stopping is safe, re-run to resume)
       xerj corpus list [--url URL]

a flag may precede the verb (xerj corpus --url URL index <name>);
clone the repos, detect licences, write corpora/<name>/corpus.json;
a repo entry may set 'paths' to relative directories (for example data/osv)
and the checkout harvests only those; omit it to harvest the whole pin, and
the list is written back into corpus.json;
a local checkout's root .xerjignore is copied into the clone when it differs
from the committed file (git clone drops an untracked or uncommitted one);
a pinned --from rebuild stays exact and does not copy it, and says so;
--from takes the corpus name from the manifest's 'corpus' field (or the
pack's 'pack' field) unless <name> or --as overrides it; a harvested pack
also checksum-verifies and materializes records per source; --verify-sig
checks the pack's SHA256SUMS.sig against a public key file first and
refuses the pack on failure (for a pack.zip, the sig cannot travel inside
— releases ship it loose beside the zip as <pack>-SHA256SUMS.sig, which
is where the lookup falls back to); build harvests recipe sources into a
deterministic pack under builds/<name>/ (see tools/xerj-code/); sign/keygen
are the publish step (ed25519 over SHA256SUMS);
index builds/verifies/switches the corpus (exit 3 skips junk — normal); it
skips CSV/HDF/simulation output by default (reference corpora are code and
docs, and a test-output folder can out-record the whole corpus) —
--include-data indexes those files too, reporting how many were left out;

content.content:
1 │ ---
  2 │ title: "ACP"
  3 │ description: "Use OpenCode with an Agent Client Protocol client."
  4 │ ---
  5 │ 
  6 │ `opencode acp` runs OpenCode as an [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) agent, so you can use it
  7 │ from an ACP client such as Zed. This example adds OpenCode to Zed:
  8 │ 
  9 │ ```json title="~/.config/zed/settings.json"
 10 │ {
 11 │   "agent_servers": {
 12 │     "OpenCode": {
 13 │       "command": "opencode",
 14 │       "args": ["acp"]
 15 │     }
 16 │   }
 17 │ }
 18 │ ```
 19 │ 
 20 │ Other ACP clients use the same command and `acp` argument, but their configuration file and field names may differ. If
 21 │ a graphical client can't find `opencode`, set `command` to the absolute path that `which opencode` prints.
 22 │ 
 23 │ ## Authentication
 24 │ 
 25 │ OpenCode uses the provider credentials it already has. Sign in from a terminal before you start the ACP client:
 26 │ 
 27 │ ```bash
 28 │ opencode auth login
 29 │ ```
 30 │ 
 31 │ OpenCode offers one auth method, `opencode-login`. By default it's an agent auth method. The `authenticate` request
 32 │ accepts only that method and doesn't collect credentials. If a prompt fails because a provider needs authentication,
 33 │ OpenCode returns ACP's `auth_required` error.
 34 │ 
 35 │ If the client sets `clientCapabilities.auth.terminal` to `true`, the auth method is a terminal auth method:
 36 │ 
 37 │ ```json
 38 │ {
 39 │   "id": "opencode-login",
 40 │   "name": "Login with opencode",
 41 │   "description": "Run `opencode auth login` in the terminal",
 42 │   "type": "terminal",
 43 │   "args": ["--login"]
 44 │ }
 45 │ ```
 46 │ 
 47 │ The client must not send this method to `authenticate`. Instead, it adds `--login` to the command that starts OpenCode,
 48 │ for example `opencode acp --login`, and runs it in a terminal. OpenCode runs the `opencode auth login` flow and exits.
 49 │ Exit status 0 means the login succeeded. The client then reconnects and sends `initialize` again.
 50 │ 
 51 │ If the client sets `clientCapabilities._meta["terminal-auth"]` to `true`, the auth method includes the login command:
 52 │ 
 53 │ ```json
 54 │ {
 55 │   "id": "opencode-login",
 56 │   "name": "Login with opencode",
 57 │   "description": "Run `opencode auth login` in the terminal",
 58 │   "_meta": { "terminal-auth": { "command": "opencode", "args": ["auth", "login"], "label": "OpenCode Login" } }
 59 │ }
 60 │ ```
 61 │ 
 62 │ ## Troubleshooting
 63 │ 
 64 │ `opencode acp` waits for ACP messages on stdin, so it looks stuck when you run it directly in a terminal. Start it from
 65 │ an ACP client instead.
 66 │ 
 67 │ If the client reports that the process exited or wrote invalid protocol output, add `--print-logs` before `acp` in the
 68 │ client's arguments. OpenCode then writes its ACP and private server logs to stderr. Stdout carries only ACP messages.
 69 │ 
 70 │ ```bash
 71 │ opencode --print-logs acp
 72 │ ```
 73 │ 
 74 │ ## Protocol reference
 75 │ 
 76 │ This section is for ACP client authors. It lists the parts of ACP that OpenCode supports and the `_meta` keys that
 77 │ OpenCode adds. Clients that don't recognize these keys can ignore them. The
 78 │ [ACP documentation](https://agentclientprotocol.com) defines the messages.
 79 │ 
 80 │ ### Transport
 81 │ 
 82 │ The client starts `opencode acp` as a child process. The two exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over stdin and
 83 │ stdout, using ACP protocol version 1.
 84 │ 
 85 │ `opencode acp` starts a private OpenCode server for its own use. It doesn't connect to the shared background service,
 86 │ and it doesn't open a network port for ACP. One process can serve many ACP sessions. It exits when the client closes
 87 │ stdin.
 88 │ 
 89 │ ### Capabilities
 90 │ 
 91 │ OpenCode's `initialize` response includes these agent capabilities:
 92 │ 
 93 │ ```json
 94 │ {
 95 │   "loadSession": true,
 96 │   "mcpCapabilities": { "http": true, "sse": false },
 97 │   "promptCapabilities": { "embeddedContext": true, "image": true },
 98 │   "sessionCapabilities": {
 99 │     "additionalDirectories": {},
100 │     "close": {},
101 │     "delete": {},
102 │     "fork": {},
103 │     "list": {},
104 │     "resume": {}
105 │   }
106 │ }
107 │ ```
108 │ 
109 │ OpenCode reads these client capabilities:
110 │ 
111 │ | Capability                             | Effect                                                         |
112 │ | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
113 │ | `auth.terminal` set to `true`          | The auth method is a [terminal auth method](#authentication).  |
114 │ | `elicitation.form`                     | OpenCode asks [questions](#questions) as forms.                |
115 │ | `session.compaction`                   | OpenCode reports [compaction](#compaction) with ACP's updates. |
116 │ | `_meta["terminal-auth"]` set to `true` | The auth method includes the [login command](#authentication). |
117 │ 
118 │ ### Sessions
119 │ 
120 │ The client sets the working directory when it creates a session. OpenCode uses that directory's configuration,
121 │ including its models, agents, commands, skills, instructions, plugins, and MCP servers.
122 │ 
123 │ - `cwd` must be an absolute path. OpenCode rejects a relative `cwd` with an invalid params error.
124 │ - `session/load` replays the saved messages. `session/resume` and `session/fork` don't replay them.
125 │ - To load, resume, or fork a session, the client must pass that session's directory as `cwd`. OpenCode rejects a
126 │   different `cwd` with an invalid params error.
127 │ - `session/list` returns up to 100 sessions per page. It accepts a `cwd` filter and a `cursor`.
128 │ - `session/close` interrupts active work and detaches the session from the ACP process. OpenCode keeps the saved
129 │   session.
130 │ - `session/delete` ends an active prompt like `session/cancel`, then removes the session. Deleting a session that
131 │   doesn't exist succeeds.
132 │ - A session runs one prompt at a time. OpenCode returns an error for a second `session/prompt` while the first is
133 │   active.
134 │ 
135 │ ### Cancellation
136 │ 
137 │ `session/cancel` ends the active prompt with `stopReason: "cancelled"`. A `$/cancel_request` for the prompt request does
138 │ the same. OpenCode rejects pending permission requests. It reports tool calls that don't finish after a cancel as
139 │ `failed`.
140 │ 
141 │ ### Additional directories
142 │ 
143 │ The client can pass `additionalDirectories` on `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, and `session/fork`:
144 │ 
145 │ ```json
146 │ { "cwd": "/work/app", "additionalDirectories": ["/work/shared"], "mcpServers": [] }
147 │ ```
148 │ 
149 │ - Each entry must be an absolute path without `*` or `?`.
150 │ - OpenCode allows external directory access inside each root. Read, edit, and shell permission rules still apply.
151 │ - Each request's list replaces the session's previous list, as the
152 │   [additional directories RFD](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/additional-directories) specifies.
153 │ - OpenCode stores the grants on the session, so they also apply when another OpenCode client uses the session. Child
154 │   sessions copy the grants when OpenCode creates them.
155 │ 
156 │ `session/list` returns each session's stored list in `additionalDirectories`.
157 │ 
158 │ ### Config options
159 │ 
160 │ New sessions use the directory's default model and primary agent. The responses to `session/new`, `session/load`,
161 │ `session/resume`, and `session/fork` include these config options:
162 │ 
163 │ | ID       | Category        | Values                                                                        |
164 │ | -------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
165 │ | `model`  | `model`         | Enabled models as `provider/model`. A `/variant` suffix also sets the effort. |
166 │ | `effort` | `thought_level` | The model's variants and `default`. Present only for models with variants.    |
167 │ | `mode`   | `mode`          | Visible primary agents.                                                       |
168 │ 
169 │ `session/set_config_option` takes string values:
170 │ 
171 │ ```json
172 │ { "sessionId": "ses_123", "configId": "model", "value": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5" }
173 │ ```
174 │ 
175 │ `session/set_mode` also sets the agent. OpenCode sends `config_option_update` when the available models or agents
176 │ change. It also sends one when another client changes the session's model or agent.
177 │ 
178 │ ### Prompt content
179 │ 
180 │ Prompts can contain text, images, embedded resources, and resource links. OpenCode ignores audio blocks. It handles the
181 │ other blocks like this:
182 │ 
183 │ | Block                                                 | What OpenCode does                                                                     |
184 │ | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
185 │ | `text`                                                | Sends it to the model.                                                                 |
186 │ | `text` with audience `assistant` only                 | Sends it to the model as separate context, outside the user's message.                 |
187 │ | `text` with audience `user` only                      | Leaves it out of the model's input.                                                    |
188 │ | `image` with `data`                                   | Attaches it to the prompt.                                                             |
189 │ | `image` with only `uri`                               | Handles it as a resource link.                                                         |
190 │ | `resource` with `text`                                | Inlines the text after the resource's path or URI.                                     |
191 │ | `resource` with `blob`                                | Attaches it if it has a `mimeType`. Drops it otherwise.                                |
192 │ | `resource_link` to a `file://` URI                    | Attaches the file. Sends a Markdown link instead if the file is missing or unreadable. |
193 │ | `resource_link` to a `zed://` URI with a `path` query | Attaches the file at `path`.                                                           |
194 │ | `resource_link` to another URI                        | Sends a Markdown link such as `[spec](https://example.com/spec.md)`.                   |
195 │ 
196 │ The audience comes from the block's `annotations`. OpenCode rejects an `image` block that has neither `data` nor `uri`.
197 │ This block is context for the model only:
198 │ 
199 │ ```json
200 │ { "type": "text", "text": "Open file: src/app.ts", "annotations": { "audience": ["assistant"] } }
201 │ ```
202 │ 
203 │ ### Commands
204 │ 
205 │ After `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, or `session/fork`, OpenCode sends `available_commands_update`
206 │ with the directory's commands and the built-in `compact` command. It sends another update when the commands change.
207 │ 
208 │ ```json
209 │ {
210 │   "sessionUpdate": "available_commands_update",
211 │   "availableCommands": [{ "name": "compact", "description": "Compact the session" }]
212 │ }
213 │ ```
214 │ 
215 │ If a prompt starts with `/` and the name of an available command, OpenCode runs that command with the rest of the text
216 │ as arguments. OpenCode sends other text that starts with `/` as a normal prompt. `/compact` runs
217 │ [compaction](/compaction).
218 │ 
219 │ ### MCP servers
220 │ 
221 │ The client can pass stdio and HTTP MCP servers on `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, and `session/fork`.
222 │ OpenCode adds them to the session's directory for the life of the `opencode acp` process, so other sessions in that
223 │ directory can use them. OpenCode passes HTTP headers through and doesn't use OAuth for these servers. It doesn't
224 │ advertise MCP over SSE, and it doesn't support MCP over ACP.
225 │ 
226 │ | Case                             | Behavior                                                            |
227 │ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
228 │ | Same name as a configured server | The client's server replaces the configured one in that directory. |
229 │ | [Policies](/policies)            | `integration.use` rules still apply.                                |
230 │ 
231 │ ```json
232 │ { "type": "http", "name": "docs", "url": "https://mcp.example.com", "headers": [] }
233 │ ```
234 │ 
235 │ ### Permissions
236 │ 
237 │ Permission requests offer three options:
238 │ 
239 │ ```json
240 │ [
241 │   { "optionId": "once", "kind": "allow_once", "name": "Allow once" },
242 │   { "optionId": "always", "kind": "allow_always", "name": "Always allow" },
243 │   { "optionId": "reject", "kind": "reject_once", "name": "Reject" }
244 │ ]
245 │ ```
246 │ 
247 │ When a request changes files, OpenCode includes `diff` content if it can build a preview of the change.
248 │ 
249 │ ### Questions
250 │ 
251 │ If the client advertises `elicitation.form`, OpenCode asks questions with `elicitation/create` in form mode. The request
252 │ includes `toolCallId` when OpenCode sent that tool call as a `session/update` for this session.
253 │ 
254 │ ```json
255 │ {
256 │   "mode": "form",
257 │   "sessionId": "ses_123",
258 │   "toolCallId": "call_1",
259 │   "message": "Which package manager?",
260 │   "requestedSchema": {
261 │     "type": "object",
262 │     "properties": { "pm": { "type": "string", "oneOf": [{ "const": "bun", "title": "Bun" }] } },
263 │     "required": ["pm"]
264 │   }
265 │ }
266 │ ```
267 │ 
268 │ - OpenCode never sends forms that might collect secrets.
269 │ - If a field accepts a typed answer next to its options, the schema adds an optional `<key>_custom` string property.
270 │   For a single choice, a non-empty custom answer replaces the selected option. For a multiple choice, OpenCode adds it
271 │   to the selected options.
272 │ - If the user declines or cancels the form, OpenCode cancels the question.
273 │ 
274 │ If OpenCode can't show a question, it cancels the question and tells the model to continue without an answer.
275 │ 
276 │ ### Compaction
277 │ 
278 │ If the client advertises `session.compaction`, OpenCode reports compaction with the `compaction_update` and
279 │ `compaction_summary_chunk` updates from ACP's [session compaction](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/session-compaction)
280 │ RFD, which is in Preview. When the client loads a session, OpenCode replays each completed or failed compaction as one
281 │ update.
282 │ 
283 │ ```json
284 │ {
285 │   "sessionUpdate": "compaction_update",
286 │   "compactionId": "msg_123",
287 │   "status": "completed",
288 │   "summary": [{ "type": "text", "text": "..." }]
289 │ }
290 │ ```
291 │ 
292 │ Other clients receive the [compaction marker](#compaction-marker) instead. So do child session compactions.
293 │ 
294 │ ### Usage
295 │ 
296 │ The prompt response includes `usage` from the [end-turn usage](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/end-turn-token-usage)
297 │ RFD, which is a draft. `usage` sums the prompt's model calls in this session. It doesn't include child sessions.
298 │ 
299 │ ```json
300 │ { "stopReason": "end_turn", "usage": { "inputTokens": 1200, "outputTokens": 340, "totalTokens": 1540 }, "_meta": {} }
301 │ ```
302 │ 
303 │ Before the response, OpenCode sends `usage_update` from the
304 │ [session usage](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/session-usage) RFD. It sends it only if the prompt used tokens and
305 │ OpenCode knows the model's context size. `cost` is the session's total cost in USD.
306 │ 
307 │ ```json
308 │ { "sessionUpdate": "usage_update", "used": 1540, "size": 200000, "cost": { "amount": 0.012, "currency": "USD" } }
309 │ ```
310 │ 
311 │ ### Child sessions
312 │ 
313 │ While a prompt runs, OpenCode sends updates from its child sessions as `session/update` notifications on the prompt's
314 │ session. Each update carries `_meta["opencode/child-session"]`. OpenCode prefixes tool call IDs with
315 │ `<childSessionId>:`. It prefixes tool call titles with the child session's title if the child session has one.
316 │ 
317 │ ```json
318 │ {
319 │   "sessionUpdate": "tool_call",
320 │   "toolCallId": "ses_child:call_1",
321 │   "title": "Explore the codebase: src/app.ts",
322 │   "_meta": {
323 │     "opencode/child-session": { "id": "ses_child", "parentID": "ses_123", "depth": 1, "title": "Explore the codebase" }
324 │   }
325 │ }
326 │ ```
327 │ 
328 │ | Field      | Type     | Description                                                                            |
329 │ | ---------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
330 │ | `id`       | `string` | The child session's ID.                                                                |
331 │ | `parentID` | `string` | The ID of the child session's parent session.                                          |
332 │ | `depth`    | `number` | 1 for a child of the prompt's session, 2 for a child of that child session, and so on. |
333 │ | `title`    | `string` | The child session's title. OpenCode omits it when the child session has no title.      |
334 │ 
335 │ Permission requests from a child session carry the same key on `toolCall._meta`. After the prompt ends, OpenCode stops
336 │ sending child session updates. Permission requests and questions from child sessions still reach the client.
337 │ 
338 │ ### Retry status
339 │ 
340 │ When a model call fails and OpenCode schedules a retry, it sends `session_info_update` with `_meta["opencode/retry"]`.
341 │ When the retry starts, OpenCode sends `"opencode/retry": null`. Clear any retry status when the prompt response arrives.
342 │ 
343 │ ```json
344 │ {
345 │   "sessionUpdate": "session_info_update",
346 │   "_meta": {
347 │     "opencode/retry": {
348 │       "attempt": 1,
349 │       "nextRetryAt": "2026-10-02T12:00:05.000Z",
350 │       "error": { "type": "provider.rate-limit", "message": "Rate limit exceeded", "status": 429 }
351 │     }
352 │   }
353 │ }
354 │ ```
355 │ 
356 │ | Field         | Type     | Description                                                                                |
357 │ | ------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
358 │ | `attempt`     | `number` | The retry attempt number.                                                                  |
359 │ | `nextRetryAt` | `string` | The time of the next attempt, in ISO 8601 format.                                          |
360 │ | `error`       | `object` | Has `type` and `message`. Also has `status` and `response.body` if the provider sent them. |
361 │ 
362 │ ### Compaction marker
363 │ 
364 │ If the client doesn't advertise `session.compaction`, OpenCode reports compaction progress as `session_info_update` with
365 │ `_meta["opencode/compaction"]`. OpenCode always uses the marker for child session compactions.
366 │ 
367 │ ```json
368 │ {
369 │   "sessionUpdate": "session_info_update",
370 │   "_meta": { "opencode/compaction": { "status": "started", "messageId": "msg_123", "reason": "auto" } }
371 │ }
372 │ ```
373 │ 
374 │ | Field       | Type     | Description                                                                          |
375 │ | ----------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
376 │ | `status`    | `string` | `started`, `completed`, or `failed`. A cancelled compaction is `failed`.             |
377 │ | `messageId` | `string` | Pairs a compaction's start with its end. Treat it as an opaque key.                  |
378 │ | `reason`    | `string` | `auto` or `manual`.                                                                  |
379 │ | `error`     | `object` | Present when `status` is `failed`. Same shape as the [retry](#retry-status) `error`. |
380 │ 
381 │ The marker doesn't include a summary. An automatic compaction can fail without a `started` marker. When the client
382 │ loads a session, OpenCode replays each completed or failed compaction as one marker.

1 │ ---
  2 │ title: "ACP"
  3 │ description: "Use OpenCode with an Agent Client Protocol client."
  4 │ ---
  5 │ 
  6 │ `opencode acp` runs OpenCode as an [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) agent, so you can use it
  7 │ from an ACP client such as Zed. This example adds OpenCode to Zed:
  8 │ 
  9 │ ```json title="~/.config/zed/settings.json"
 10 │ {
 11 │   "agent_servers": {
 12 │     "OpenCode": {
 13 │       "command": "opencode",
 14 │       "args": ["acp"]
 15 │     }
 16 │   }
 17 │ }
 18 │ ```
 19 │ 
 20 │ Other ACP clients use the same command and `acp` argument, but their configuration file and field names may differ. If
 21 │ a graphical client can't find `opencode`, set `command` to the absolute path that `which opencode` prints.
 22 │ 
 23 │ ## Authentication
 24 │ 
 25 │ OpenCode uses the provider credentials it already has. Sign in from a terminal before you start the ACP client:
 26 │ 
 27 │ ```bash
 28 │ opencode auth login
 29 │ ```
 30 │ 
 31 │ OpenCode offers one auth method, `opencode-login`. By default it's an agent auth method. The `authenticate` request
 32 │ accepts only that method and doesn't collect credentials. If a prompt fails because a provider needs authentication,
 33 │ OpenCode returns ACP's `auth_required` error.
 34 │ 
 35 │ If the client sets `clientCapabilities.auth.terminal` to `true`, the auth method is a terminal auth method:
 36 │ 
 37 │ ```json
 38 │ {
 39 │   "id": "opencode-login",
 40 │   "name": "Login with opencode",
 41 │   "description": "Run `opencode auth login` in the terminal",
 42 │   "type": "terminal",
 43 │   "args": ["--login"]
 44 │ }
 45 │ ```
 46 │ 
 47 │ The client must not send this method to `authenticate`. Instead, it adds `--login` to the command that starts OpenCode,
 48 │ for example `opencode acp --login`, and runs it in a terminal. OpenCode runs the `opencode auth login` flow and exits.
 49 │ Exit status 0 means the login succeeded. The client then reconnects and sends `initialize` again.
 50 │ 
 51 │ If the client sets `clientCapabilities._meta["terminal-auth"]` to `true`, the auth method includes the login command:
 52 │ 
 53 │ ```json
 54 │ {
 55 │   "id": "opencode-login",
 56 │   "name": "Login with opencode",
 57 │   "description": "Run `opencode auth login` in the terminal",
 58 │   "_meta": { "terminal-auth": { "command": "opencode", "args": ["auth", "login"], "label": "OpenCode Login" } }
 59 │ }
 60 │ ```
 61 │ 
 62 │ ## Troubleshooting
 63 │ 
 64 │ `opencode acp` waits for ACP messages on stdin, so it looks stuck when you run it directly in a terminal. Start it from
 65 │ an ACP client instead.
 66 │ 
 67 │ If the client reports that the process exited or wrote invalid protocol output, add `--print-logs` before `acp` in the
 68 │ client's arguments. OpenCode then writes its ACP and private server logs to stderr. Stdout carries only ACP messages.
 69 │ 
 70 │ ```bash
 71 │ opencode --print-logs acp
 72 │ ```
 73 │ 
 74 │ ## Protocol reference
 75 │ 
 76 │ This section is for ACP client authors. It lists the parts of ACP that OpenCode supports and the `_meta` keys that
 77 │ OpenCode adds. Clients that don't recognize these keys can ignore them. The
 78 │ [ACP documentation](https://agentclientprotocol.com) defines the messages.
 79 │ 
 80 │ ### Transport
 81 │ 
 82 │ The client starts `opencode acp` as a child process. The two exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over stdin and
 83 │ stdout, using ACP protocol version 1.
 84 │ 
 85 │ `opencode acp` starts a private OpenCode server for its own use. It doesn't connect to the shared background service,
 86 │ and it doesn't open a network port for ACP. One process can serve many ACP sessions. It exits when the client closes
 87 │ stdin.
 88 │ 
 89 │ ### Capabilities
 90 │ 
 91 │ OpenCode's `initialize` response includes these agent capabilities:
 92 │ 
 93 │ ```json
 94 │ {
 95 │   "loadSession": true,
 96 │   "mcpCapabilities": { "http": true, "sse": false },
 97 │   "promptCapabilities": { "embeddedContext": true, "image": true },
 98 │   "sessionCapabilities": {
 99 │     "additionalDirectories": {},
100 │     "close": {},
101 │     "delete": {},
102 │     "fork": {},
103 │     "list": {},
104 │     "resume": {}
105 │   }
106 │ }
107 │ ```
108 │ 
109 │ OpenCode reads these client capabilities:
110 │ 
111 │ | Capability                             | Effect                                                         |
112 │ | -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
113 │ | `auth.terminal` set to `true`          | The auth method is a [terminal auth method](#authentication).  |
114 │ | `elicitation.form`                     | OpenCode asks [questions](#questions) as forms.                |
115 │ | `session.compaction`                   | OpenCode reports [compaction](#compaction) with ACP's updates. |
116 │ | `_meta["terminal-auth"]` set to `true` | The auth method includes the [login command](#authentication). |
117 │ 
118 │ ### Sessions
119 │ 
120 │ The client sets the working directory when it creates a session. OpenCode uses that directory's configuration,
121 │ including its models, agents, commands, skills, instructions, plugins, and MCP servers.
122 │ 
123 │ - `cwd` must be an absolute path. OpenCode rejects a relative `cwd` with an invalid params error.
124 │ - `session/load` replays the saved messages. `session/resume` and `session/fork` don't replay them.
125 │ - To load, resume, or fork a session, the client must pass that session's directory as `cwd`. OpenCode rejects a
126 │   different `cwd` with an invalid params error.
127 │ - `session/list` returns up to 100 sessions per page. It accepts a `cwd` filter and a `cursor`.
128 │ - `session/close` interrupts active work and detaches the session from the ACP process. OpenCode keeps the saved
129 │   session.
130 │ - `session/delete` ends an active prompt like `session/cancel`, then removes the session. Deleting a session that
131 │   doesn't exist succeeds.
132 │ - A session runs one prompt at a time. OpenCode returns an error for a second `session/prompt` while the first is
133 │   active.
134 │ 
135 │ ### Cancellation
136 │ 
137 │ `session/cancel` ends the active prompt with `stopReason: "cancelled"`. A `$/cancel_request` for the prompt request does
138 │ the same. OpenCode rejects pending permission requests. It reports tool calls that don't finish after a cancel as
139 │ `failed`.
140 │ 
141 │ ### Additional directories
142 │ 
143 │ The client can pass `additionalDirectories` on `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, and `session/fork`:
144 │ 
145 │ ```json
146 │ { "cwd": "/work/app", "additionalDirectories": ["/work/shared"], "mcpServers": [] }
147 │ ```
148 │ 
149 │ - Each entry must be an absolute path without `*` or `?`.
150 │ - OpenCode allows external directory access inside each root. Read, edit, and shell permission rules still apply.
151 │ - Each request's list replaces the session's previous list, as the
152 │   [additional directories RFD](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/additional-directories) specifies.
153 │ - OpenCode stores the grants on the session, so they also apply when another OpenCode client uses the session. Child
154 │   sessions copy the grants when OpenCode creates them.
155 │ 
156 │ `session/list` returns each session's stored list in `additionalDirectories`.
157 │ 
158 │ ### Config options
159 │ 
160 │ New sessions use the directory's default model and primary agent. The responses to `session/new`, `session/load`,
161 │ `session/resume`, and `session/fork` include these config options:
162 │ 
163 │ | ID       | Category        | Values                                                                        |
164 │ | -------- | --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
165 │ | `model`  | `model`         | Enabled models as `provider/model`. A `/variant` suffix also sets the effort. |
166 │ | `effort` | `thought_level` | The model's variants and `default`. Present only for models with variants.    |
167 │ | `mode`   | `mode`          | Visible primary agents.                                                       |
168 │ 
169 │ `session/set_config_option` takes string values:
170 │ 
171 │ ```json
172 │ { "sessionId": "ses_123", "configId": "model", "value": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5-5" }
173 │ ```
174 │ 
175 │ `session/set_mode` also sets the agent. OpenCode sends `config_option_update` when the available models or agents
176 │ change. It also sends one when another client changes the session's model or agent.
177 │ 
178 │ ### Prompt content
179 │ 
180 │ Prompts can contain text, images, embedded resources, and resource links. OpenCode ignores audio blocks. It handles the
181 │ other blocks like this:
182 │ 
183 │ | Block                                                 | What OpenCode does                                                                     |
184 │ | ----------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
185 │ | `text`                                                | Sends it to the model.                                                                 |
186 │ | `text` with audience `assistant` only                 | Sends it to the model as separate context, outside the user's message.                 |
187 │ | `text` with audience `user` only                      | Leaves it out of the model's input.                                                    |
188 │ | `image` with `data`                                   | Attaches it to the prompt.                                                             |
189 │ | `image` with only `uri`                               | Handles it as a resource link.                                                         |
190 │ | `resource` with `text`                                | Inlines the text after the resource's path or URI.                                     |
191 │ | `resource` with `blob`                                | Attaches it if it has a `mimeType`. Drops it otherwise.                                |
192 │ | `resource_link` to a `file://` URI                    | Attaches the file. Sends a Markdown link instead if the file is missing or unreadable. |
193 │ | `resource_link` to a `zed://` URI with a `path` query | Attaches the file at `path`.                                                           |
194 │ | `resource_link` to another URI                        | Sends a Markdown link such as `[spec](https://example.com/spec.md)`.                   |
195 │ 
196 │ The audience comes from the block's `annotations`. OpenCode rejects an `image` block that has neither `data` nor `uri`.
197 │ This block is context for the model only:
198 │ 
199 │ ```json
200 │ { "type": "text", "text": "Open file: src/app.ts", "annotations": { "audience": ["assistant"] } }
201 │ ```
202 │ 
203 │ ### Commands
204 │ 
205 │ After `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, or `session/fork`, OpenCode sends `available_commands_update`
206 │ with the directory's commands and the built-in `compact` command. It sends another update when the commands change.
207 │ 
208 │ ```json
209 │ {
210 │   "sessionUpdate": "available_commands_update",
211 │   "availableCommands": [{ "name": "compact", "description": "Compact the session" }]
212 │ }
213 │ ```
214 │ 
215 │ If a prompt starts with `/` and the name of an available command, OpenCode runs that command with the rest of the text
216 │ as arguments. OpenCode sends other text that starts with `/` as a normal prompt. `/compact` runs
217 │ [compaction](/compaction).
218 │ 
219 │ ### MCP servers
220 │ 
221 │ The client can pass stdio and HTTP MCP servers on `session/new`, `session/load`, `session/resume`, and `session/fork`.
222 │ OpenCode adds them to the session's directory for the life of the `opencode acp` process, so other sessions in that
223 │ directory can use them. OpenCode passes HTTP headers through and doesn't use OAuth for these servers. It doesn't
224 │ advertise MCP over SSE, and it doesn't support MCP over ACP.
225 │ 
226 │ | Case                             | Behavior                                                            |
227 │ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
228 │ | Same name as a configured server | The client's server replaces the configured one in that directory. |
229 │ | [Policies](/policies)            | `integration.use` rules still apply.                                |
230 │ 
231 │ ```json
232 │ { "type": "http", "name": "docs", "url": "https://mcp.example.com", "headers": [] }
233 │ ```
234 │ 
235 │ ### Permissions
236 │ 
237 │ Permission requests offer three options:
238 │ 
239 │ ```json
240 │ [
241 │   { "optionId": "once", "kind": "allow_once", "name": "Allow once" },
242 │   { "optionId": "always", "kind": "allow_always", "name": "Always allow" },
243 │   { "optionId": "reject", "kind": "reject_once", "name": "Reject" }
244 │ ]
245 │ ```
246 │ 
247 │ When a request changes files, OpenCode includes `diff` content if it can build a preview of the change.
248 │ 
249 │ ### Questions
250 │ 
251 │ If the client advertises `elicitation.form`, OpenCode asks questions with `elicitation/create` in form mode. The request
252 │ includes `toolCallId` when OpenCode sent that tool call as a `session/update` for this session.
253 │ 
254 │ ```json
255 │ {
256 │   "mode": "form",
257 │   "sessionId": "ses_123",
258 │   "toolCallId": "call_1",
259 │   "message": "Which package manager?",
260 │   "requestedSchema": {
261 │     "type": "object",
262 │     "properties": { "pm": { "type": "string", "oneOf": [{ "const": "bun", "title": "Bun" }] } },
263 │     "required": ["pm"]
264 │   }
265 │ }
266 │ ```
267 │ 
268 │ - OpenCode never sends forms that might collect secrets.
269 │ - If a field accepts a typed answer next to its options, the schema adds an optional `<key>_custom` string property.
270 │   For a single choice, a non-empty custom answer replaces the selected option. For a multiple choice, OpenCode adds it
271 │   to the selected options.
272 │ - If the user declines or cancels the form, OpenCode cancels the question.
273 │ 
274 │ If OpenCode can't show a question, it cancels the question and tells the model to continue without an answer.
275 │ 
276 │ ### Compaction
277 │ 
278 │ If the client advertises `session.compaction`, OpenCode reports compaction with the `compaction_update` and
279 │ `compaction_summary_chunk` updates from ACP's [session compaction](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/session-compaction)
280 │ RFD, which is in Preview. When the client loads a session, OpenCode replays each completed or failed compaction as one
281 │ update.
282 │ 
283 │ ```json
284 │ {
285 │   "sessionUpdate": "compaction_update",
286 │   "compactionId": "msg_123",
287 │   "status": "completed",
288 │   "summary": [{ "type": "text", "text": "..." }]
289 │ }
290 │ ```
291 │ 
292 │ Other clients receive the [compaction marker](#compaction-marker) instead. So do child session compactions.
293 │ 
294 │ ### Usage
295 │ 
296 │ The prompt response includes `usage` from the [end-turn usage](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/end-turn-token-usage)
297 │ RFD, which is a draft. `usage` sums the prompt's model calls in this session. It doesn't include child sessions.
298 │ 
299 │ ```json
300 │ { "stopReason": "end_turn", "usage": { "inputTokens": 1200, "outputTokens": 340, "totalTokens": 1540 }, "_meta": {} }
301 │ ```
302 │ 
303 │ Before the response, OpenCode sends `usage_update` from the
304 │ [session usage](https://agentclientprotocol.com/rfds/session-usage) RFD. It sends it only if the prompt used tokens and
305 │ OpenCode knows the model's context size. `cost` is the session's total cost in USD.
306 │ 
307 │ ```json
308 │ { "sessionUpdate": "usage_update", "used": 1540, "size": 200000, "cost": { "amount": 0.012, "currency": "USD" } }
309 │ ```
310 │ 
311 │ ### Child sessions
312 │ 
313 │ While a prompt runs, OpenCode sends updates from its child sessions as `session/update` notifications on the prompt's
314 │ session. Each update carries `_meta["opencode/child-session"]`. OpenCode prefixes tool call IDs with
315 │ `<childSessionId>:`. It prefixes tool call titles with the child session's title if the child session has one.
316 │ 
317 │ ```json
318 │ {
319 │   "sessionUpdate": "tool_call",
320 │   "toolCallId": "ses_child:call_1",
321 │   "title": "Explore the codebase: src/app.ts",
322 │   "_meta": {
323 │     "opencode/child-session": { "id": "ses_child", "parentID": "ses_123", "depth": 1, "title": "Explore the codebase" }
324 │   }
325 │ }
326 │ ```
327 │ 
328 │ | Field      | Type     | Description                                                                            |
329 │ | ---------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
330 │ | `id`       | `string` | The child session's ID.                                                                |
331 │ | `parentID` | `string` | The ID of the child session's parent session.                                          |
332 │ | `depth`    | `number` | 1 for a child of the prompt's session, 2 for a child of that child session, and so on. |
333 │ | `title`    | `string` | The child session's title. OpenCode omits it when the child session has no title.      |
334 │ 
335 │ Permission requests from a child session carry the same key on `toolCall._meta`. After the prompt ends, OpenCode stops
336 │ sending child session updates. Permission requests and questions from child sessions still reach the client.
337 │ 
338 │ ### Retry status
339 │ 
340 │ When a model call fails and OpenCode schedules a retry, it sends `session_info_update` with `_meta["opencode/retry"]`.
341 │ When the retry starts, OpenCode sends `"opencode/retry": null`. Clear any retry status when the prompt response arrives.
342 │ 
343 │ ```json
344 │ {
345 │   "sessionUpdate": "session_info_update",
346 │   "_meta": {
347 │     "opencode/retry": {
348 │       "attempt": 1,
349 │       "nextRetryAt": "2026-10-02T12:00:05.000Z",
350 │       "error": { "type": "provider.rate-limit", "message": "Rate limit exceeded", "status": 429 }
351 │     }
352 │   }
353 │ }
354 │ ```
355 │ 
356 │ | Field         | Type     | Description                                                                                |
357 │ | ------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
358 │ | `attempt`     | `number` | The retry attempt number.                                                                  |
359 │ | `nextRetryAt` | `string` | The time of the next attempt, in ISO 8601 format.                                          |
360 │ | `error`       | `object` | Has `type` and `message`. Also has `status` and `response.body` if the provider sent them. |
361 │ 
362 │ ### Compaction marker
363 │ 
364 │ If the client doesn't advertise `session.compaction`, OpenCode reports compaction progress as `session_info_update` with
365 │ `_meta["opencode/compaction"]`. OpenCode always uses the marker for child session compactions.
366 │ 
367 │ ```json
368 │ {
369 │   "sessionUpdate": "session_info_update",
370 │   "_meta": { "opencode/compaction": { "status": "started", "messageId": "msg_123", "reason": "auto" } }
371 │ }
372 │ ```
373 │ 
374 │ | Field       | Type     | Description                                                                          |
375 │ | ----------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
376 │ | `status`    | `string` | `started`, `completed`, or `failed`. A cancelled compaction is `failed`.             |
377 │ | `messageId` | `string` | Pairs a compaction's start with its end. Treat it as an opaque key.                  |
378 │ | `reason`    | `string` | `auto` or `manual`.                                                                  |
379 │ | `error`     | `object` | Present when `status` is `failed`. Same shape as the [retry](#retry-status) `error`. |
380 │ 
381 │ The marker doesn't include a summary. An automatic compaction can fail without a `started` marker. When the client
382 │ loads a session, OpenCode replays each completed or failed compaction as one marker.

 25 │ // Untraced so request spans parent to the caller's span instead of a setup span that has already ended.

 51 │         }),

 53 │         Effect.tapCauseIf(Cause.hasDies, (cause) => Effect.logError("ACP request failed", cause)),
 54 │         Effect.catchDefect((defect) => Effect.fail(ACPError.toRequestError(ACPError.fromUnknown(defect)))),
 55 │       )

 57 │     }

32 │ export function make(app: AgentApp, stream: Stream) {
33 │   const responses = new Map<JsonRpcId, Deferred.Deferred<void>>()
34 │   const writer = stream.writable.getWriter()
35 │   const agent = app.connect({
36 │     readable: stream.readable,
37 │     writable: new WritableStream<AnyMessage>({
38 │       write: async (message) => {
39 │         await writer.write(message)
40 │         if ("method" in message) return
41 │         const responded = responses.get(message.id)
42 │         if (!responded) return
43 │         responses.delete(message.id)
44 │         Deferred.doneUnsafe(responded, "result" in message ? Effect.void : Effect.interrupt)
45 │       },
46 │       close: () => writer.close(),
47 │       abort: (reason) => writer.abort(reason),
48 │     }),
49 │   })

51 │     agent,
52 │     connection: {
53 │       sessionUpdate: (params) => promise(() => agent.client.notify(methods.client.session.update, params)),
54 │       requestPermission: (params) =>
55 │         promise((signal) =>

62 │         ),

65 │         responses.set(requestId, responded)

"""ACP permission bridging for Hermes dangerous-command approvals."""

from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import logging
from concurrent.futures import TimeoutError as FutureTimeout
from itertools import count
from typing import Callable

from acp.schema import (
    AllowedOutcome,
    PermissionOption,
)

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

# Maps ACP permission option ids to Hermes approval result strings.
# Option ids are stable across both the ``allow_permanent=True`` and
# ``allow_permanent=False`` paths even though the option list differs.
_OPTION_ID_TO_HERMES = {
    "allow_once": "once",
    "allow_session": "session",
    "allow_always": "always",
    "deny": "deny",
    "deny_always": "deny",
}

_PERMISSION_REQUEST_IDS = count(1)


def _permission_option_supports_kind(kind: str) -> bool:
    """Return whether the installed ACP SDK accepts a permission option kind."""
    try:
        PermissionOption(option_id="__probe__", kind=kind, name="probe")
    except Exception:
        return False
    return True


def _build_permission_options(*, allow_permanent: bool) -> list[PermissionOption]:
    """Return ACP options that match Hermes approval semantics."""
    options = [
        PermissionOption(option_id="allow_once", kind="allow_once", name="Allow once"),
        PermissionOption(
            option_id="allow_session",
            # ACP has no session-scoped kind, so use the closest persistent
            # hint while keeping Hermes semantics in the option id.
            kind="allow_always",
            name="Allow for session",
        ),
    ]
    if allow_permanent:
        options.append(
            PermissionOption(
                option_id="allow_always",
                kind="allow_always",
                name="Allow always",
            ),
        )
    options.append(PermissionOption(option_id="deny", kind="reject_once", name="Deny"))
    if _permission_option_supports_kind("reject_always"):
        options.append(
            PermissionOption(
                option_id="deny_always",
                kind="reject_always",
                name="Deny always",
            ),
        )
    return options


def _build_permission_tool_call(command: str, description: str):
    """Return the ACP tool-call update attached to a permission request.

    ``request_permission`` expects a ``ToolCallUpdate`` payload — produced
    by ``_acp.update_tool_call`` — not a ``ToolCallStart``. Each request
    gets a unique ``perm-check-N`` id so concurrent requests don't collide.
    """
    import acp as _acp

    tool_call_id = f"perm-check-{next(_PERMISSION_REQUEST_IDS)}"
    title = f"{description}: {command}" if description else command
    content_text = f"{description}\n$ {command}" if description else f"$ {command}"
    return _acp.update_tool_call(
        tool_call_id,
        title=title,
        kind="execute",
        status="pending",
        content=[_acp.tool_content(_acp.text_block(content_text))],
        raw_input={"command": command, "description": description},
    )


def _map_outcome_to_hermes(outcome: object, *, allowed_option_ids: set[str]) -> str:
    """Map an ACP permission outcome into Hermes approval strings."""
    if not isinstance(outcome, AllowedOutcome):
        return "deny"

    option_id = outcome.option_id
    if option_id not in allowed_option_ids:
        logger.warning("Permission request returned unknown option_id: %s", option_id)
        return "deny"
    return _OPTION_ID_TO_HERMES.get(option_id, "deny")


def make_approval_callback(
    request_permission_fn: Callable,
    loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop,
    session_id: str,
    timeout: float = 60.0,
) -> Callable[..., str]:
    """
    Return a Hermes-compatible approval callback that bridges to ACP.

    The callback accepts ``command`` and ``description`` plus optional
    keyword arguments such as ``allow_permanent`` used by
    ``tools.approval.prompt_dangerous_approval()``.

    Args:
        request_permission_fn: The ACP connection's ``request_permission`` coroutine.
        loop: The event loop on which the ACP connection lives.
        session_id: Current ACP session id.
        timeout: Seconds to wait for a response before auto-denying.
    """

    def _callback(
        command: str,
        description: str,
        *,
        allow_permanent: bool = True,
        **_: object,
    ) -> str:
        from agent.async_utils import safe_schedule_threadsafe

        options = _build_permission_options(allow_permanent=allow_permanent)

        tool_call = _build_permission_tool_call(command, description)
        coro = request_permission_fn(
            session_id=session_id,
            tool_call=tool_call,
            options=options,
        )
        future = safe_schedule_threadsafe(
            coro, loop,
            logger=logger,
            log_message="Permission request: failed to schedule on loop",
        )
        if future is None:
            return "deny"

## What the protocol covers, and what it does not

A client starts the sidecar as a child process and talks to it over the child's standard input and output. That is the only transport.

Not part of this protocol today:

- No socket or network transport. A client cannot attach to a sidecar that another process started (planned as PF-3).
- No library entry point. The sidecar is a process, not an importable API (planned as PF-4).
- No Agent Client Protocol (ACP). This is Nexus's own protocol (ACP is planned as AC-1).

The sidecar projects the agent's state. It never asks the client to decide an outcome: whether a turn succeeded, whether a change is verified and whether a tool call is allowed are decided in the sidecar and reported. The one thing a client is asked for is a human's answer: yes or no to an `approval.request`, and a choice for a `checkpoint.choice.request`. An approval request is raised by the side

## Transport and framing

- The sidecar is the Node program `cli/dist/sidecar.js` (in an installed release, `lib/cli/dist/sidecar.js` under the Nexus home). Run it with `--help` for its options: endpoint, model, workspace, approval mode, `--resume`.
- The client writes commands to the sidecar's stdin and reads events from its stdout. Stdout carries protocol lines only. Stderr carries diagnostics for a log, in no fixed format.
- Each message is one JSON object on one line, UTF-8, ended by `\n` (newline-delimited JSON). A newline inside a string is escaped, as JSON requires. The sidecar ignores blank lines and accepts `\r\n`.
- Every message, in both directions, carries `v` (the protocol version, an integer) and `type` (a string that names the message).
- A string the sidecar sends is well-formed Unicode: a lone UTF-16 surrogate, which cutting a text can leave behind, is sent as U+FFFD.

### Sizes

The sidecar bounds the free-text fields of its events, counted in UTF-16 code units, and a text cut at its limit usually ends with `…[truncated N chars]`:

| Limit | Applies to |
|---|---|
| 8,000 (`MAX_TEXT_FIELD`) | most free text: `notice.text` and `detail`, `error.message`, `turn.result.heading` and `line`, `tool.start.subject`, `approval.request.subject` and `preview`, `steer.ack.message`, `slash.result.prompt`, `provider.auth.instructions`, the `message` of `provider.result` and `model.result` |
| 64,000 | `assistant.delta.text`, `steer.ack.text`, `tool.detail.args` and `output` |
| 256,000 | `tool.detail.diff` |
| 32,000 (`MAX_SLASH_OUTPUT`) | `slash.result.output` |
| 100,000 (`MAX_PASTE`) | `slash.result.composer` |
| 160 (`MAX_SUMMARY`) | `tool.end.summary` |

The Nexus terminal UI treats a stdout line longer than 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) as not a protocol event and drops it. The limits above bound the text fields they name; `turn.result` and `models.catalog` carry structured data with no stated cap, so this page does not promise that every event line stays below that size. A client may apply the same cap and should treat an over-long line as one dropped

The sidecar sets no limit on the length of a line it reads. It does limit some command fields: `initialize` accepts `client.name` and `client.version` of at most 100 characters and version bounds from 1 to 65,535, and `provider.connect` accepts an `endpoint` of at most 2,048 characters on a single line.

## Start-up and shut-down

1. The client starts the sidecar.
2. The sidecar sends `hello`, always first, and then `session.state`. After `--resume`, a `history` event (the restored conversation) comes between the two. `notice` events may follow, for example when no model provider answers.
3. The client may send `initialize` (see Negotiation). It does not have to.
4. The client sends commands; the sidecar sends events, some in answer to a command and some on its own.
5. The client sends `shutdown`, or closes the sidecar's stdin, which the sidecar treats as `shutdown`. The sidecar interrupts a running turn and exits with status 0.

Commands may be sent at any time after `hello`, including while a turn runs. The sidecar handles them in the order received.

## Versioning

- `PROTOCOL_VERSION` (1) is the version the sidecar speaks by default: the `v` of every event, and the `protocol` field of `hello`.
- The sidecar can speak an inclusive range of versions, `PROTOCOL_MIN` to `PROTOCOL_MAX`, announced in `hello` as `protocol_min` and `protocol_max`. Today the range is 1 to 1.
- The sidecar accepts a command whose `v` is an integer inside that range. Any other `v` is refused with `error` / `BAD_REQUEST` ("unsupported protocol version").
- Within one version, changes are additive: a new optional field on an existing message, a new event type, a new command, a new error code, a new capability name. An additive change never removes a field, never changes the type or meaning of an existing field, and never makes an optional field required. A peer written before the change keeps working because of the compatibility rules below.
- Anything else is a breaking change and needs a new protocol version: `PROTOCOL_VERSION` is raised, the range `PROTOCOL_MIN` to `PROTOCOL_MAX` says which versions the sidecar still speaks, and a new schema file `protocol/sidecar-v<N>.schema.json` is published.
- Every change to the protocol types is recorded. [`protocol/VERSIONS.json`](protocol/VERSIONS.json) is a ledger whose newest entry must carry the SHA-256 of the checked-in schema and the current version, with a note that states the decision (additive, same version; or a new version). CI fails when a type changes and the schema and ledger do not. [`protocol/README.md`](protocol/README.md) describe

- Within one version, changes are additive: a new optional field on an existing message, a new event type, a new command, a new error code, a new capability name. An additive change never removes a field, never changes the type or meaning of an existing field, and never makes an optional field required. A peer written before the change keeps working because of the compatibility rules below.
- Anything else is a breaking change and needs a new protocol version: `PROTOCOL_VERSION` is raised, the range `PROTOCOL_MIN` to `PROTOCOL_MAX` says which versions the sidecar still speaks, and a new schema file `protocol/sidecar-v<N>.schema.json` is published.
- Every change to the protocol types is recorded. [`protocol/VERSIONS.json`](protocol/VERSIONS.json) is a ledger whose newest entry must carry the SHA-256 of the checked-in schema and the current version, with a note that states the decision (additive, same version; or a new version). CI fails when a type changes and the schema and ledger do not. [`protocol/README.md`](protocol/README.md) describe
